title: Paging through big tables
summary: Why OFFSET gets slower and skips rows, and keyset pagination with a tie-breaker.

steps.title: OFFSET reads everything it skips
setup: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, event_id INTEGER NOT NULL, customer TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 20000) INSERT INTO orders SELECT i, i % 5 + 1, 'customer' || ((i * 7919) % 3000) || '@mail.test', i % 4 + 1, datetime('2026-09-01', '+' || (i * 6) || ' minutes', '+' || ((i * 37) % 3) || ' seconds') FROM n;
CREATE INDEX orders_placed ON orders (placed_at, id);
body: The box office's order list pages like this:
```sql
SELECT id, placed_at FROM orders
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000;     -- page 501

`OFFSET 10000` does not jump anywhere: the database walks 10,020 rows in order and throws the first 10,000 away. Page 1 is fast, page 500 is slow, and the export job that walks every page does quadratic work.
Worse, it is wrong while data changes: an order placed between two page loads shifts every row down by one, so the next page **repeats** a row; a deleted order makes it **skip** one.
**Keyset pagination** (also called the seek method) remembers where the last page ended and asks for the rows after it. With an index on the sort columns, that is a jump to a spot in the index:
```sql
SELECT id, placed_at FROM orders
WHERE (placed_at, id) < ('2026-10-12 20:00:01', 10021)   -- the last row of the previous page
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
Compare what SQLite really does for both, on 20,000 orders:

setup: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, event_id INTEGER NOT NULL, customer TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 20000) INSERT INTO orders SELECT i, i % 5 + 1, 'customer' || ((i * 7919) % 3000) || '@mail.test', i % 4 + 1, datetime('2026-09-01', '+' || (i * 6) || ' minutes', '+' || ((i * 37) % 3) || ' seconds') FROM n;
CREATE INDEX orders_placed ON orders (placed_at, id);
sqlplan.query: SELECT id, placed_at FROM orders ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000
sqlplan.after: SELECT id, placed_at FROM orders WHERE (placed_at, id) < ('2026-10-12 20:00:01', 10021) ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20
sqlplan.note: Same index, same 20 rows. The plans look alike (both walk the index backwards); the work does not: OFFSET steps through every skipped entry.

steps.prompt: A customer is on page 3 of their order history (20 per page, `OFFSET 40`). While they read it, a new order of theirs is placed. They click *Next*. What do they see?
options: The last order of page 3 again at the top of page 4
An error, because the result changed
steps.explain: The new order goes to the top (newest first), pushing every row down by one, so `OFFSET 60` now starts one row earlier. A keyset query starts after the last row actually shown, so inserts and deletes elsewhere do not move it.

steps.title: The tie-breaker
body: Keyset paging needs an order in which **every row has a unique position**. `placed_at` alone is not unique: three orders came in at 09:12. If a page ends in the middle of them, `WHERE placed_at > '2026-11-20 09:12'` skips the rest of that minute.
So sort by the column you want **plus a unique column** (usually the id), and compare both at once with a **row value**:
```sql fragment
ORDER BY placed_at, id
Row values compare like words in a dictionary: first `placed_at`, and `id` only when the times are equal. PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and SQLite 3.15+ support them. **SQL Server does not**; write it out:
```sql fragment
WHERE placed_at > @lastAt OR (placed_at = @lastAt AND id > @lastId)

The index must match the sort, `(placed_at, id)`, and the API hands the client an opaque cursor (often base64 of `placed_at` and `id`) instead of a page number. Step through the page after `(09:12, 4)` below: order 5 and 6 share 09:12 but come after id 4, so they are kept.

setup: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL);

steps.prompt: SQL Server has no row-value comparison. Complete the "next page" condition for `ORDER BY placed_at, id`.
steps.explain: Strictly later time, or the same time with a larger id. Using `>=` in the first part would repeat rows from the same minute.

steps.title: The next page
prompt: The order list is sorted **oldest first** by `placed_at`, then `id`. Page 1 ended with the order placed at **`2026-11-20 08:18:00`** with id **12**.
Return the **next 10** orders: **id**, **customer**, **placed_at**, using a keyset condition (no OFFSET).
Table: `orders(id, customer, placed_at)` (60 rows; several orders share a `placed_at` minute), with an index on `(placed_at, id)`.
setup: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 60) INSERT INTO orders SELECT i, 'customer' || ((i * 17) % 40) || '@mail.test', datetime('2026-11-20 08:00', '+' || ((i / 2) * 3) || ' minutes') FROM n;
CREATE INDEX orders_placed ON orders (placed_at, id);
hints: Same ORDER BY as the list, `placed_at, id`, then `LIMIT 10`. The ▤ Query plan button shows it searching the index.
steps.explain: Order 13 shares the 08:18 minute with order 12 and still appears first: that is the tie-breaker doing its job.

steps.prompt: Which screen is the better fit for plain `LIMIT ... OFFSET`?
options: An admin table of 300 venues with numbered pages and "jump to page 7"
An infinite-scroll feed of 40 million orders, newest first
A nightly export that walks every order in batches of 5,000
An API that clients page through while new rows keep arriving
steps.explain: Small and fairly static data, where users want page numbers: OFFSET is simple and fine. Deep, growing or changing data wants keyset. (Keyset cannot jump to page 7 directly; that is its trade-off.)

steps.title: Newest first, page 2
prompt: The same list, now **newest first** (`placed_at DESC, id DESC`). The first page ended with the order at **`2026-11-20 08:57:00`**, id **38**.
Return the **next 10** orders (**id**, **customer**, **placed_at**) with a keyset condition.
Table: `orders(id, customer, placed_at)` (60 rows; several orders share a `placed_at` minute), with an index on `(placed_at, id)`.
solution: ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
setup: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, placed_at TEXT NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 60) INSERT INTO orders SELECT i, 'customer' || ((i * 17) % 40) || '@mail.test', datetime('2026-11-20 08:00', '+' || ((i / 2) * 3) || ' minutes') FROM n;
CREATE INDEX orders_placed ON orders (placed_at, id);
hints: Going backwards in time, "after" means smaller: `<`.
`WHERE (placed_at, id) < ('2026-11-20 08:57:00', 38) ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10`
steps.explain: Flip the comparison with the sort direction. Both columns must sort the same way for a single row-value comparison to work; a mixed sort (`placed_at DESC, id ASC`) needs the written-out OR form.
